extracted.intended_audience: Contributors to the Metamath Proof Explorer / authors of the set.mm database (theorem/axiom definers)
extracted.subtask_description: Conventions and rules for choosing and formatting labels for axioms, definitions, theorems, hypotheses, and related items in the Metamath Proof Explorer (set.mm). Guidance covers allowed characters, fragments, suffixes, reuse, and examples.

rubrics_metrics.name: Unique identifying label
rubrics_metrics.description: Every statement has a unique identifying label, which serves the same purpose as an equation number in a book.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Labels uniquely identify statements in set.mm and should be used consistently; treat labels as the canonical short identifier for a theorem/axiom/definition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Labels should be short and suggestive (not 1-to-1 mapping)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use label naming conventions to provide easy-to-remember hints about their contents. Labels are not a 1-to-1 mapping (that would create long names); instead, labels are relatively short while suggesting their purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer shorter, unambiguous labels rather than fully descriptive long names. Names may be changed later for consistency or clarity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Axioms, proven-axiom proofs, definitions, and wff syntax naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Axioms are named 'ax-NAME', proofs of proven axioms are named 'axNAME', and definitions are named 'df-NAME'. Wff syntax declarations begin with 'w' followed by a short fragment suggesting purpose.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow these prefixes to distinguish axioms (ax-), proofs-of-axioms (axNAME), definitions (df-), and wff syntax (w*).

rubrics_metrics.name: Hypotheses labeling convention
rubrics_metrics.description: Hypotheses have the name of the final axiom or theorem, followed by '.', followed by a unique id (usually consecutive integers starting at 1) or letters corresponding to the main class variable used in the hypothesis.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'rgen.1 $e |- ( x e. A -> ph ) $.'; or use letter suffixes like 'mdet0.d' where the suffix letter corresponds to a class variable. Periods in labels are normally used only for hypotheses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of common/well-known theorem names
rubrics_metrics.description: If a theorem has a well-known name, that name (or a short version of it) is sometimes used directly as the label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'barbara', 'stirling'. Use recognizable short names when appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Principia Mathematica theorem naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Proofs of theorems from Principia Mathematica often use the naming convention 'pm' followed by its identifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Theorem *2.27 of Whitehead & Russell p.104 is named 'pm2.27'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Margaris Section 19 ('19.x') naming
rubrics_metrics.description: Theorems from Section 19 of Margaris often use the naming convention '19.' (or 'r19.' for restricted quantifier versions) followed by the identifier.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: Theorem 38 from Section 19 of Margaris is labeled '19.38'; restricted quantifier version 'r19.21'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Allowed characters and case
rubrics_metrics.description: Although Metamath allows dots/periods in any label, they are usually used only in hypothesis labels; the underscore '_' should not be used. Only lower-case characters should be used (except special suffixes OLD, ALT, ALTV). Exceptions are tolerated in mathboxes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid underscores and uppercase letters in main set.mm labels. Reserve periods for hypothesis labels and the specific exceptions noted (e.g., 'pm' and '19.x').

rubrics_metrics.name: Syntax label fragments (concatenation)
rubrics_metrics.description: Most theorems are named by concatenating syntax label fragments (omitting variables) that represent the important part of the theorem's main conclusion. Almost every syntactic construct has a definition 'df-NAME' and NAME is normally the syntax fragment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance:
Examples: class difference df-dif -> fragment 'dif'; subclass relation df-ss -> fragment 'ss'; theorem proving (A 
 B) ⊆ A is labeled 'difss'. Digits represent themselves; use suffixes or numbers to disambiguate collisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Phantom definitions (fragments without df-NAME)
rubrics_metrics.description: Some common constructs lack a df-NAME definition but still have a syntax fragment used in labels (phantom definitions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: element-of '∈' does not have df-NAME but uses fragment 'el' (e.g., 'eldifsn'). Negation often uses 'n' (e.g., 'nan').

rubrics_metrics.name: Exceptions to fragment=NAME and documenting them
rubrics_metrics.description: Sometimes there is a df-NAME but the label fragment is not NAME; the definition should note this exception and the conventions page lists many such cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: 'cn' denotes complex numbers though defined in df-c; 're' denotes real numbers though defined in df-r; empty set often uses '0' despite df-nul; 'p' used for constant theorems; equality often uses 'e'. Definitions that deviate should explicitly mention the exception.

rubrics_metrics.name: Other marking fragments (semantic abbreviations)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use short fragments for common properties/operations like 'com' for commutative, 'ass' for associative, 'rot' for rotation, and 'di' for distributive.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These fragments are appended to labels to indicate such properties (e.g., 'orcom', 'mulass').

rubrics_metrics.name: Label focus: emphasize the conclusion
rubrics_metrics.description: A label typically provides a hint about the conclusion only; it rarely says anything about the hypotheses or antecedents. If multiple theorems have the same conclusion but different hypotheses, labels should differ to emphasize the differences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No need to fully describe the conclusion—identify the important part. Prefer concise unambiguous labels (e.g., 'cos0' instead of 'cos0eq1') when disambiguation is unnecessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: Closures and values naming for functions
rubrics_metrics.description: When a function is defined by df-NAME, there is typically a proof of its value labeled 'NAMEval' and a proof of its closure labeled 'NAMEcl'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: for df-cos we have 'cosval' and 'coscl'. Follow this pattern for function definitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Special-case and propositional-calculus naming
rubrics_metrics.description: When syntax fragments are insufficient to distinguish many theorems (e.g., many implication-only theorems), group them ad-hoc using abbreviations like 'mp' (modus ponens), 'syl' (syllogism), 'id' (identity) or parametric series (e.g., 'syl*anc', 'simp*').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Propositional calculus section is hard to name; rely on a few very common labels and parametric series; search set.mm for existing labels before inventing new ones.

rubrics_metrics.name: Suffixes indicate theorem form and conditions
rubrics_metrics.description: Suffixes are used to indicate the form of a theorem (inference, deduction, or closed form) and other conditions. Examples include 'v' (disjoint variable condition), 'f' (not free in / introduces hypothesis), 'b' (biconditional), 's' (eliminates syllogism), 'a' (conjunction antecedent), 'd' (deduction form), 'i' (inference form), 't' (closed form), 'w' (weaker form), and multi-suffix combinations; 'ALT','ALTV','OLD' mark alternate or obsolete versions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ordering rule: suffixes for theorem forms ('i','d','g') should be first when combining with others (e.g., 'vtocldf' = v + t + o + c + l + d + f example). The page lists a non-exhaustive catalog of common suffixes and example usages; combine suffixes as needed (e.g., 'vv', 'vvv' for multiple disjoint-variable conditions).

rubrics_metrics.name: Try to reuse abbreviations and document first use
rubrics_metrics.description: When creating a new theorem or axiom, try to reuse abbreviations used elsewhere. A comment should explain the first use of an abbreviation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Reusing existing abbreviations improves consistency and discoverability; always add a comment on first use to define the abbreviation in context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Common abbreviations table (reference list)
rubrics_metrics.description: The page provides a (non-exhaustive) alphabetical table of commonly used abbreviations/fragments, giving a mnemonic, source, expression, whether it's a syntax fragment, and label examples.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this table as the canonical reference for which fragments/abbreviations are preferred (e.g., 'dif' for set difference df-dif, 'ss' for subset df-ss, 'sn' for singleton df-sn, 'pr' for pair df-pr, 'cn' for complex numbers, 're' for reals, etc.). The table is intended to be expanded toward completeness; consult it before introducing new fragments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Document revisions and discourage proof modification/new usage
rubrics_metrics.description: The page records date of contribution and revision; proof modification is discouraged and new usage is discouraged unless necessary.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect the historical and consistency notes (e.g., 'Proof modification is discouraged.' 'New usage is discouraged.'); prefer to adhere to established conventions rather than introduce new naming patterns without good reason.
